html:
The Caliphate of Córdoba was the Umayyad state of al-Andalus, Muslim Spain, at its height, from 929 to 1031. It is shown here in 1000. Its capital, Córdoba, was then one of the largest and richest cities in Europe.

The state was founded in 756 as an emirate by Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid massacre of his family. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph, rejecting both the Abbasids and the new Fatimid Caliphate in North Africa. He built the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra, and his son al-Hakam II gathered a huge library and enlarged the Great Mosque.

From 978 the real ruler was the chamberlain al-Mansur, who raided the Christian north more than fifty times and sacked Santiago de Compostela in 997. After his sons died, civil war, the Fitna of al-Andalus, broke out in 1009. The caliphate was abolished in 1031, and al-Andalus split into small taifa kingdoms.
